title: Distributed Commit Log
prompt: Design a distributed message log like Kafka. Producers append messages to named topics. Many independent consumer groups read them in order, at their own pace, and can replay history.

clarify.q: Do consumers need to replay old messages, or is a message gone once acknowledged?
clarify.why: Replay means the log is the storage: messages stay for days no matter who read them, and consumers track a position. A classic work queue deletes on ack instead.

clarify.q: What ordering guarantee: global, per key, or none?
clarify.why: Global order means one writer for everything, which caps throughput at one machine. Per-key order lets us split a topic into partitions and scale out.

clarify.q: Throughput and message size, average and peak?
clarify.why: Bytes per second decide broker count, partition count and whether disk or network is the limit.

clarify.q: Can we ever lose an acknowledged message?
clarify.why: Zero loss needs synchronous replication before ack and refusing writes when too few replicas are healthy. That trades availability for durability during failures.

clarify.q: How long is data kept, and do some topics only need the latest value per key?
clarify.why: Time retention drives disk sizing. Latest-per-key topics (changelog, config) need compaction instead of deletion.
Synchronous replication across regions adds tens of ms to every write. Most designs replicate within a region and mirror asynchronously between regions.
Exactly-once needs idempotent producers and transactions that commit output and consumer offsets together, which adds a coordinator and latency.

functional: Producers append messages (key, value, headers) to a topic; messages with the same key keep their order.
Consumers in a group share a topic's partitions; each message goes to one member of each group.
Different groups read the same data independently; a group can rewind to an offset or a timestamp.
Per-topic retention by time or size, and optional log compaction that keeps the latest value per key.
Producers can choose durability per write: no ack, leader ack, or all in-sync replicas ack.
nonFunctional: Sustain 1.5 GB/s produce at peak and 3 consumer groups reading everything.
With acks=all, no acknowledged message is lost when any single broker fails.
Produce p99 under 20 ms with acks=all in one region; end-to-end p99 under 50 ms for caught-up consumers.
Broker failure: affected partitions get a new leader within ~5 s.
Consumers far behind must not slow down producers or caught-up consumers.
outOfScope: Per-message routing rules, priorities and delayed delivery (classic broker features).
Schema registry and stream-processing frameworks on top.
Multi-region active-active writes to the same topic.
Client library ergonomics beyond the wire protocol.

assumptions: Average message 1 KB including key and headers
3 consumer groups read every topic on average
Brokers with 20 TB usable disk and 25 Gbps NICs

steps.label: Produce bandwidth
steps.math: 500 k/s × 1 KB = 500 MB/s; peak 1.5 M/s × 1 KB = 1.5 GB/s

steps.label: Retained data
steps.math: 500 MB/s × 604 800 s (7 days) ≈ 302 TB; × 3 replicas ≈ 907 TB

steps.label: Brokers if all data stays local
Peak network across the cluster
steps.math: in: 1.5 produce + 3.0 replication = 4.5 GB/s; out: 3.0 replication + 4.5 consumers (3 × 1.5) = 7.5 GB/s
steps.result: Over 46 brokers ≈ 163 MB/s out each, ~1.3 Gbps: network is not the limit

steps.label: With tiered storage (1 day local)
steps.math: 500 MB/s × 86 400 ≈ 43 TB; × 3 ≈ 130 TB local; 7.5 GB/s / 12 brokers ≈ 625 MB/s ≈ 5 Gbps out each
steps.result: ≈ 12 brokers, now sized by network; old segments in object storage

steps.label: Partitions for a 300 MB/s topic
steps.math: 300 MB/s / 5 MB/s per consumer instance = 60; × 2 for growth
steps.result: 120 partitions; key-to-partition mapping is fixed once chosen

steps.label: Producer batching
steps.math: 1.5 M msg/s / 64 messages per 64 KB batch ≈ 23 k batches/s
steps.result: ≈ 23 k requests/s cluster-wide: batching is what makes this cheap

estimates.takeaway:
With seven days kept locally, disk decides the cluster size (~46 brokers) and the network is mostly idle. Moving segments older than a day to object storage cuts the fleet to ~12 brokers, and then network fan-out to consumer groups is the limit. That is a clear trade: cheaper brokers, but replaying old data is slower and depends on the object store.

Per-request overhead is negligible only because producers batch. Without batching we would face 1.5 M requests/s. Partition count comes from consumer parallelism, not broker throughput, and it is hard to change later for keyed topics.

api.path: Produce(topic, partition, records[], acks, producerId, epoch, baseSequence)
api.returns: { baseOffset, logAppendTime } or error NOT_LEADER | NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS
api.note: Records arrive as a compressed batch. producerId + sequence lets the leader drop duplicates from retries.

api.path: Fetch(topic, partition, offset, maxBytes, maxWaitMs, isolation)
api.note: Long poll: the broker holds the request up to maxWaitMs until data arrives. Followers use the same call to replicate.
Group coordinator assigns partitions. A stale generation is rejected, which fences zombie consumers.
Stored in an internal compacted topic keyed by (group, topic, partition).

api.returns: { brokers[], partitions: [{ id, leader, replicas, isr, leaderEpoch }] }
api.note: Clients cache this and refresh on NOT_LEADER errors.
For exactly-once read-process-write. Output records and consumer offsets commit atomically.

entities.name: Partition log segment
entities.store: Broker local disk, then object storage after 1 day
fields: segment file named by its first offset
[offset, timestamp, key, value, headers], compressed per batch
then roll to a new segment
entities.why: Append-only files. Writes are sequential, and reads by offset are a seek plus a sequential read, usually served from page cache.

entities.name: Offset index and time index
entities.why: Sparse indexes: find the nearest entry by binary search, then scan forward a few KB. Small enough to keep in memory for every segment.

entities.name: Partition state
entities.why: Small, strongly consistent metadata. A 3- or 5-node Raft quorum owns it so there is exactly one truth about who leads each partition.

entities.name: Consumer group offsets
entities.why: Offsets are just messages in a log, so they get replication and compaction for free. The coordinator for a group is the leader of the offsets partition that the group ID hashes to.

data.note:
The design splits data plane from control plane. Message bytes live in partition logs replicated leader-to-followers, with no consensus round per message. Who leads which partition, and the ISR list, lives in a small Raft-replicated metadata log run by a controller quorum.

This split is why throughput scales with brokers while metadata stays strongly consistent. The data plane gets its safety from the ISR rules plus leader epochs, which are decided by the control plane.

hld.summary:
A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log with one leader and two followers on different brokers and racks. Producers hash the key to pick a partition and send batches to its leader. The leader appends to its log, and followers fetch from the leader the same way consumers do. Once every in-sync replica has a batch, the leader advances the high watermark, and only data below it is visible to consumers.

A controller quorum (Raft) stores cluster metadata: topics, partition leaders, ISR and leader epochs. It reassigns leaders when a broker dies. Consumer groups talk to a group coordinator broker that assigns partitions to members and stores committed offsets in an internal compacted topic. A tiering job copies closed segments to object storage, and brokers serve old offsets from there.

  CQ -.-> F2

flows.title: Producing with acks=all
steps: Producer batches records per partition for up to ~5 ms or 64 KB, compresses the batch, and sends it to the partition leader.
Leader checks producerId and sequence to drop duplicates, then appends the batch to the active segment (page cache, no fsync per write).
Followers' pending Fetch requests return the new batch; each follower appends and fetches again from its new end offset.
When all ISR members have reached that offset, the leader moves the high watermark and acknowledges the producer.
If the ISR has shrunk below min.insync.replicas (2), the leader rejects the write with NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS instead of accepting it unsafely.

flows.title: Consuming in a group
steps: Consumer finds its group coordinator, joins, and receives a generation number and a set of partitions.
For each partition it reads the committed offset and sends Fetch from there; the broker long-polls until data is available.
Broker sends bytes from page cache straight to the socket (zero-copy) when no conversion is needed.
Consumer processes the batch, then commits the next offset with its generation; a stale generation is rejected.

flows.title: A broker dies
steps: Controller notices missed heartbeats after ~5 s and marks the broker dead.
For each partition it led, controller picks a new leader from the remaining ISR, bumps the leader epoch, and writes this to the metadata log.
Brokers and clients learn the new leaders; producers retry their in-flight batches, which idempotence makes safe.
When the old broker returns, it truncates its log to the point agreed with the new leader for its last epoch, then catches up as a follower.

deepDives.title: Storage: why an append-only partitioned log is fast
deepDives.problem: We need ~1.5 GB/s of writes and ~4.5 GB/s of consumer reads, with consumers at very different positions. A classic queue that keeps per-message state and deletes on ack does random I/O and bookkeeping per message, which collapses at this rate.

options.name: Per-message queue with acks and deletes
options.how: Store messages in a B-tree or database table; mark each acked and delete it.
pros: Per-message redelivery, priorities and delays are easy
Storage shrinks as messages are consumed
cons: Random writes plus per-message state updates
Replay of history is impossible once deleted
Each consumer group needs its own copy

options.name: Partitioned append-only log
options.how: Each partition is a sequence of segment files written only at the end. Consumers keep a single integer offset per partition.
pros: Sequential writes and reads, mostly from page cache
Any number of groups share one copy; replay is just a smaller offset
Retention deletes whole segment files, which is cheap
cons: Ordering only within a partition
One slow message blocks its partition for that group (head-of-line)
No per-message ack or redelivery; that has to be built on top

deepDives.choice:
The partitioned log. Four things make it fast. Batches are written as-is, so the broker never parses individual messages. Writes go to the OS page cache and durability comes from replication, not fsync. Reads by caught-up consumers hit page cache and use zero-copy sendfile. Sparse offset indexes stay in memory.

The cost is that a far-behind consumer reads cold data from disk or object storage, and that can evict hot pages. Tiered storage and separate read throttles protect caught-up readers. If the workload needed per-message retries, priorities or delays (a job queue), I would put a classic broker in front or build a retry-topic pattern rather than bend the log.

deepDives.title: Replication: ISR, high watermark and acks
deepDives.problem: Every partition has three copies. We must decide when a write counts as committed, who may become leader after a crash, and what happens when replicas fall behind. Quorum-per-message (Paxos/Raft) costs a consensus round per batch. Waiting for every replica lets one slow disk stall the partition.

options.name: acks=0 or acks=1
options.how: Producer does not wait, or waits only for the leader's local append.
pros: Lowest latency
Unaffected by slow followers
cons: acks=1 loses acked data if the leader dies before followers copy it
acks=0 loses data silently on any error

options.name: acks=all with an in-sync replica set
options.how: Leader tracks which followers are caught up (ISR). A write is committed when all current ISR members have it. Slow followers are dropped from the ISR after ~30 s behind and rejoin when caught up. min.insync.replicas=2 sets the floor.
pros: Survives any one broker failure with no loss
A slow follower is removed instead of stalling writes
No per-batch consensus round, just follower fetches
cons: Latency is the slowest ISR member's fetch round trip
If ISR drops below 2, writes to that partition fail (choosing consistency over availability)

options.name: Majority quorum per partition (Raft)
options.how: Each partition is its own Raft group; commit when a majority has the entry.
pros: Tolerates a slow minority without changing membership
Well-understood safety proofs
cons: Needs 2f+1 replicas to tolerate f failures (ISR needs f+1)
Per-partition Raft state for tens of thousands of partitions is heavy

deepDives.choice:
ISR with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 on a replication factor of 3, with replicas spread across racks or zones. One broker can fail with no loss and no write outage. With two down, writes stop rather than risk loss. That is the CAP choice for durable topics; a metrics topic could choose acks=1 instead.

Two details matter in an interview. First, consumers only see data below the high watermark, so they never read something that could be rolled back. Second, the leader epoch stamps each batch. After a failover, a returning ex-leader asks the new leader where its last epoch ended and truncates any un-committed tail. Without this, the replicas can silently diverge. Unclean leader election (promoting an out-of-sync replica) is off by default; turning it on trades data loss for availability.

deepDives.title: Consumer groups and rebalancing
deepDives.problem: A group of N consumers must split P partitions so each partition has exactly one owner. Membership changes all the time: deploys, autoscaling, crashes, long GC pauses. During a rebalance, partitions can stall. Worse, a consumer that was presumed dead may come back and keep committing offsets or writing output.

options.name: Stop-the-world (eager) rebalance
options.how: On any change every member revokes all partitions, rejoins, and gets a fresh assignment.
pros: Simple to reason about
No partition is ever owned by two members
cons: Whole group pauses on every change, often for seconds
Rolling deploy of 50 consumers causes 50 full pauses

options.name: Incremental (cooperative) rebalance
options.how: Members keep partitions that do not move; only partitions being reassigned are revoked, over two short rounds.
pros: Most partitions keep flowing during deploys
Pairs well with sticky assignment
cons: Two rounds instead of one
More complex client protocol

options.name: Static membership
options.how: Each consumer has a stable instance ID; a restart within a session timeout reclaims the same partitions without a rebalance.
pros: Rolling restarts cause no rebalance at all
Keeps local caches and state warm
cons: A truly dead member is noticed only after the longer timeout

deepDives.choice:
Cooperative rebalancing with sticky assignment, plus static membership for stateful consumers. Fencing comes from the generation number: every commit carries it, and the coordinator rejects commits from an old generation. That stops a zombie from overwriting offsets.

Fencing output (not just offsets) needs transactions, covered next. Parallelism is capped at the partition count: 120 partitions means at most 120 active members per group. If a team needs more parallelism than partitions, they process within a partition with a per-key worker pool and commit the lowest fully processed offset.

deepDives.title: Offsets and delivery semantics
deepDives.problem: Producers retry on timeouts, and consumers crash between processing and committing. Without care you get duplicates (at-least-once) or losses (at-most-once). People ask for exactly-once, but it only holds within boundaries we control.

options.name: At-most-once
options.how: Consumer commits the offset before processing.
pros: Never processes twice
cons: A crash after commit and before processing loses messages

options.name: At-least-once plus idempotent handlers
options.how: Process, then commit. Handlers dedupe by a message key or upsert by ID.
pros: No loss; simple broker
Works with any external sink that supports upserts
cons: Every handler must be idempotent
Duplicates after a crash: up to one batch per partition

options.name: Exactly-once within the log
options.how: Idempotent producer (producerId + per-partition sequence numbers, so the leader drops retried batches) plus transactions: output records and the input offsets commit atomically via a transaction coordinator. Readers use read_committed and skip aborted data.
pros: Read-process-write between topics has no duplicates or losses
Zombie producers are fenced by an epoch on a stable transactional ID
cons: Extra latency per transaction (commit markers, coordinator round trips)
Only covers sinks that are topics in this log; an external database still needs idempotent writes

deepDives.choice:
Turn on the idempotent producer by default; it is nearly free and removes retry duplicates. For consumers, default to at-least-once with idempotent handlers, because most sinks are external databases where log transactions do not reach.

Offer transactions for stream-processing jobs that read and write topics in this log; commit every ~100 ms to amortise the cost. Say it plainly: exactly-once is a property of a closed system. At its edge, you need an idempotent or transactional sink.

deepDives.title: Retention, compaction and tiered storage
deepDives.problem: Disk is finite, but different topics need different lifetimes. Events should be kept for seven days. A topic holding the latest profile per user should keep one record per key forever. Replays of last month's data should not need petabytes of broker disk.

options.name: Delete by time or size
options.how: When a closed segment's newest record is older than retention, delete the file.
pros: O(1) per segment, no rewriting
Predictable disk use
cons: Old data is gone even if it is the only copy of a key's latest value

options.name: Log compaction
options.how: A background cleaner rewrites old segments keeping only the newest record per key. A null value (tombstone) deletes a key and is itself removed after a grace period.
pros: Topic becomes a durable, replayable table: new consumers rebuild state from it
Disk is bounded by key count, not by write rate
cons: Cleaner I/O and memory (a key-to-offset map)
Only the latest value survives, so history is lost
Offsets become sparse; consumers must handle gaps

options.name: Tiered storage
options.how: Closed segments are copied to object storage; brokers keep ~1 day locally and fetch older ranges remotely.
pros: Broker count drops from ~46 to ~12 in our numbers
Long retention becomes cheap; replacing a broker means copying 1 day, not 7
cons: Old reads are slower (object storage latency) and depend on another system
More moving parts in the fetch path

deepDives.choice:
All three, chosen per topic. Event topics use 7-day time retention with tiered storage, so brokers hold one day. Changelog and offset topics use compaction. The internal offsets topic is compacted too, which is why committed offsets never grow without bound.

Tombstones must live longer than the slowest consumer's lag, or a consumer that is a day behind will miss the delete. I would set that grace period to at least the longest lag any consumer is allowed to have, for example 24 h. If the object store had poor availability, I would keep more days local and accept the bigger fleet.

failures: Controller elects a new leader from the ISR and bumps the epoch; producers retry and idempotence drops duplicates; acked writes were on all ISR members, so none are lost.
It falls out of the ISR after the lag timeout, so writes keep committing with 2 replicas; alert, then replace the disk and let it catch up.
ISR below min.insync.replicas: acks=all writes fail fast. Consistency is chosen over availability; acks=1 topics keep accepting writes.
Network partition isolates the old leader
It cannot reach the controller, so it is replaced; its stale epoch makes followers and clients reject it. Any un-replicated tail it wrote is truncated when it rejoins.
A consumer group falls days behind and reads cold data
Serve from tiered storage with per-client read quotas so cold reads cannot evict hot pages; alert on lag in time, not just in messages.
Raft with 3 or 5 nodes keeps working with a majority; data-plane reads and writes continue even while metadata is briefly unavailable, but no leader changes can happen.
scale: 10× throughput: network becomes the limit. Add brokers, rebalance partition leaders, enable fetch-from-nearest-replica for consumers so they read from a follower in their zone, and use stronger batch compression.
100 k+ partitions: metadata and failover time grow. Keep metadata in the Raft log with snapshots, push incremental metadata updates to brokers, and discourage tiny topics with many partitions.
Multi-region: keep each cluster regional and mirror topics asynchronously with offset translation. Active-active on one topic needs conflict handling at the application level.
Cost: tiered storage turns broker count from a disk problem into a network problem; past that, the next lever is moving consumers to read replicas in their own zone to cut cross-zone traffic charges.

followups.q: Why not use Raft for every partition instead of ISR?
answer: Raft needs a majority, so tolerating 1 failure costs 3 replicas and 2 failures costs 5; ISR tolerates f failures with f+1 replicas.
ISR has no per-batch voting: followers just fetch, which is cheap at high throughput.
The trade-off: ISR depends on a separate consistent controller to decide membership, and that is where we use Raft.

followups.q: How do you add partitions to a keyed topic without breaking order?
answer: Adding partitions changes hash(key) mod P, so a key's new messages land on a different partition than its old ones.
Safe path: create a new topic with more partitions, dual-write or migrate, and switch consumers at a known offset.
Lesson: choose a generous partition count up front for keyed topics.

followups.q: How does a consumer seek to 'yesterday at 9 am'?
answer: Each segment has a time index mapping timestamps to offsets.
Broker binary-searches segments by their max timestamp, then the time index, and returns the first offset at or after that time.
Consumer commits that offset and fetches normally.

followups.q: How would you implement a delay or retry queue on this?
answer: Failed messages go to a retry topic per delay tier (1 min, 10 min) with a not-before timestamp.
A consumer on each tier waits until the timestamp before reprocessing; after N tries, a dead-letter topic.
This preserves the main partition's flow instead of blocking on one bad message.

followups.q: What does the broker do when a consumer is slow?
answer: Nothing; the consumer just has a lower offset. Data stays until retention.
If lag exceeds retention, the consumer loses data, so alert on lag as time-until-loss.
Quotas cap how hard a catching-up consumer can pull so it does not hurt others.

mistakes: Promising global ordering across a topic while also promising horizontal scale.
Saying 'exactly-once' without naming the idempotent producer, transactions, and the limit at external sinks.
Letting consumers read past the high watermark, then being surprised by data that disappears after a failover.
Using a consensus round per message, or not explaining how the leader is chosen and fenced.
Sizing brokers by throughput alone and forgetting that seven days of retention at 3 copies is ~0.9 PB.

mid: Explained topics, partitions, offsets and why ordering is per partition
Stated that consumers track an offset and messages are not deleted on read
Estimated bandwidth and storage including the replication factor
Described consumer groups sharing partitions, one owner per partition
senior: Explained ISR, high watermark and what acks=0/1/all each risk
Set min.insync.replicas and described what happens when the ISR shrinks below it
Compared eager and cooperative rebalancing and explained generation-based fencing
Placed the commit before or after processing and named the resulting semantics
Distinguished time retention from compaction and named tombstones
staff: Separated control plane (Raft metadata) from data plane (ISR replication) and justified the split
Explained leader epochs and log truncation after failover
Described the idempotent producer and transactions, and said exactly-once stops at external sinks
Used the numbers to show tiered storage turns a disk-bound fleet into a network-bound one
Discussed partition count as a near-permanent choice for keyed topics
